Learning Objectives
Describe relevant peripheral nerve anatomy.
Explain different degrees of nerve injury.
List appropriate imaging or nerve conduction studies in evaluating nerve injury or dysfunction.
Review principles of nerve repair and the anticipated timeline of nerve recovery.
Peripheral Nervous System
Function
Peripheral nerves connect the central nervous system (CNS) with tissues such as bone, joints,
muscles, tendons, and skin.
Nerves that supply the musculoskeletal system provide motor and sensory function.

Structure and Composition
Neuronal Anatomy
Every neuron contains a cell body, which is its metabolic center.
The cell bodies of most neurons also give rise to one long branch, known as an axon, and to
several short branches, known as dendrites (Figure 1, A).
Dendrites are thin nerve processes that receive input from other nerves.
The axon is the primary distal projection of the cell body of the neuron.
The neuron conveys signals to tissues and to other nerve cells via the axon, which conveys
action potentials to the other cells.
The neuron receives messages from other neurons via its dendrites, which convey action
potentials from the axons of the other neurons.
The axon of a neuron meets the dendrites of one or more adjoining neurons at a junction
called the synapse, the location at which action potentials from the axon pass into the
dendrites of the other neurons.
Axons typically are 0.2 to 20.0 μm in diameter and arise from an axon hillock, which initiates
the action potentials of neurons.
Myelin, which is composed of fatty substances and proteins, forms an insulating sheath
around the axons of neurons in the peripheral nervous system. The myelin that forms this
sheath is produced by Schwann cells, which belong to a larger family of nonneuronal cells
known as glial cells. A function of myelin is to speed the conduction of action potentials along
the axons of nerve cells.
In unmyelinated nerve fibers, a single Schwann cell envelops multiple axons, and conduction
proceeds more slowly than in myelinated nerve fibers, in which each axon is
circumferentially laminated by a Schwann cell. In unmyelinated and myelinated nerve fibers,
the Schwann cells neighbor one another along the length of the fiber.
The nodes of Ranvier are interruptions or gaps between segments of the myelin sheath; they
permit the propagation of action potentials.
Myelinated axons conduct action potentials faster than unmyelinated fibers.
Compressive neuropathies and other demyelinating conditions, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth
disease, affect myelin.
As an axon reaches its end organ, it divides into fine terminal branches with specialized
endings called presynaptic terminals, which are responsible for transmitting a signal to
postsynaptic receptors (Figure 1).

Nerve Anatomy
Nerve fibers are collections of axons with Schwann cell sheaths surrounding them.

Afferent nerve fibers convey information from sensory receptors to the CNS.
Efferent nerve fibers transmit signals from the CNS to muscle and other tissue in the periphery
of the body (ie, outside the brain and spinal cord).
Nerve fibers have been classified based on their size and conduction velocity (Table 1).

Nerve Anatomy
The afferent system includes sensory innervation, translating various forms of stimuli
into electrical signals. Sensory receptors can be rapidly adapting, with a short response
to a maintained stimulation, or slowly adapting, with a response that lasts until
stimulation ceases. The efferent system includes motor innervation to skeletal and
smooth muscle, with large, myelinated axons that release acetylcholine at
neuromuscular junctions. A motor unit is a group of skeletal muscle fibers innervated by
a single neuron. During muscle contraction, the smallest motor units are the first to fire,

and additional motor units are recruited in order of increasing size until adequate force
is generated; this recruitment can be observed with electromyography (EMG).1
Composition
A nerve consists of collections of nerve fibers called fascicles and of neural connective tissue,
which surrounds and lies within each fascicle (Figure 2).
The axons within a fascicle are surrounded by a connective tissue layer called endoneurium.
Endoneurium is primarily composed of a collagenous matrix with fibroblasts, mast cells, and
capillaries and forms a bilaminar sheath around the axon, Schwann cells, and myelin of a
nerve fiber.
Perineurium is a thin, dense connective tissue layer that surrounds the fascicles of a nerve.
It has a high tensile strength and maintains interfascicular pressure, providing a barrier to
perineurial diffusion. This barrier limits injury to nerve fibers by limiting diffusion of the
epineurial edema fluid that occurs in stretch and compression injuries. The barrier created
by the perineurium also limits the diffusion of endoneurial edema fluid that can occur if a
nerve is compressed.
Spinal nerve roots have less perineurium than peripheral nerves and are more susceptible
to stretch and compression injury.
Epineurium is a supportive sheath that contains multiple groups of fascicles. It also contains
a well-developed network of extrinsic, interconnected blood vessels that run parallel to the
fascicles.

Composition
Peripheral nerves are composed of organized groups of nerve fascicles that form nerve
branches to innervate end organs. Fascicles within a nerve are larger and fewer in
number in more proximal locations; they are smaller and greater in number distally. In
the proximal extremity, the nerve fibers that supply the proximal limb tend to be more
superficially located within the nerve to facilitate branching to their target compared
with more distally directed fibers that are distributed over multiple fascicles. As the
nerve reorganizes distally, nerve fibers with the same distal target join the same
fascicles. Fascicles become superficially positioned before branching, and terminal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:29 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002111
6/36

branches often are monofascicular. Distally, fascicles are cable-like and can be followed
proximally for a considerable distance with consistent somatic organization. Eventually,
fascicles will begin to intermingle with other fascicles proximally and will become less
discrete. The ability to follow well-defined fascicles for a substantial distance proximally
is the basis for nerve transfer surgery. Historically, it was thought that fascicles
frequently redistribute by branching and uniting with other fascicle branches, resulting
in a constantly changing plexiform architecture. Sunderland believed that any given
fascicular pattern would not persist for more than 1.5 cm; however, more recent studies
have shown that although nerve fascicles intermingle proximally, far less intermingling
occurs than previously reported by Sunderland.1 These more recent studies also have
shown that nerve fibers that innervate specific end organs typically remain together
along much of the nerve course, even throughout fascicular rearrangements
proximally.1
The structural organization of fascicles changes throughout the length of a nerve.
Fascicles do not run as isolated, parallel strands from the spinal cord to a
presynaptic terminal or end organ. The number and size of fascicles change as
fascicular plexuses unite and divide within a nerve (Figure 3).
At the joint level, the fascicles of a nerve are numerous and are smaller to
accommodate nerve deformation as the joint goes through a range of motion. For
example, the ulnar nerve at the elbow contains many small fascicles, which minimize
injury to this nerve with elbow flexion and extension.
In contrast to the ulnar nerve, the radial nerve at the level of the spiral groove has a
small number of large fascicles, which do not tolerate stretch well. This level-specific
internal anatomy places the radial nerve at greater risk for neurapraxia if it is
mobilized and retracted from the spiral groove.
Sunderland initially described that fascicles frequently redistribute by branching and
uniting with other fascicle branches and that a particular fascicular pattern would not
stay constant for more than 1.5 cm;1-4 more recent studies has demonstrated that
fascicular patterns stay more constant despite some early fascicular branching
proximally.5

Blood Supply
A peripheral nerve has intrinsic and extrinsic vessels, with multiple anastomoses between one
another throughout the length of the nerve.
At the epineural level, no blood-nerve barrier exists. 
At the capillary level within the endoneurium, a blood-nerve barrier exists, similar to the
blood-brain barrier. This barrier prevents the diffusion of many different macromolecules
into the nerve, maintaining neural integrity. The blood-nerve diffusion barrier can be
damaged by infection, radiation, or metabolic disease.

Blood Supply
The vascular network of the nerve can be divided into a segmental extrinsic system that
enters from the mesoneurium and a longitudinal intrinsic system present in the
epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium. The macrocirculation, or vasa nervorum,
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Biology and Function of Nerve

consists of segmental vessels that enter the epineurium and split into ascending and
descending branches that travel along the length of the nerve. These vessels lie in a
coiled orientation with excess length, which prevents vessel injury during nerve gliding
and excursion. The segmental vessels anastomose within the interfascicular epineurium
and send branches through the perineurium and endoneurium to supply the
microcirculation of the endoneurial space. The density of capillaries within the
endoneurial space is proportional to the local metabolic demands, with fewer capillaries
supplying peripheral nerves compared with sites of neuronal cell bodies. Lymphatic
vessels travel adjacent to blood vessels within the epineurium. Epineurial arterioles and
venules are permeable to macromolecules, allowing them to enter the epineurial
interstitial space, the location at which they are removed by lymphatics.1
Nerve Endings
Afferent nerve fibers use specific primary receptors to collect sensory information from the
periphery. Three types of sensory information and four attributes of the sensory information

Mechanoreceptors: three types

Nerve Endings
The afferent system includes sensory innervation, translating various forms of stimuli
into electrical signals. Sensory receptors can be rapidly adapting, with a short response
to a maintained stimulation, or slowly adapting, with a response that lasts until

AAOS | Biology and Function of Nerve
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002111
10/36

stimulation ceases. A receptive field is the cutaneous area that a single neuron
innervates; areas with smaller receptive fields, such as the fingertips, have superior
stimuli discrimination. Tactile mechanoreceptors are present in the dermis, fascia, and
periosteum and allow for interpretation of physical stimuli, such as pressure, vibration,
and position. These include slowly adapting Merkel cells that sense constant touch,
quickly adapting Meissner corpuscles that sense moving touch, and quickly adapting
Pacinian corpuscles that sense vibration. Innervation density can be evaluated via static
and moving two-point discrimination to evaluate Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles,
respectively. Threshold sensory detection can be evaluated with the use of tuning forks
to assess threshold vibration detected by Pacinian corpuscles and with the use of
Semmes-Weinstein monofilament to assess threshold touch detected by Merkel cells.
Proprioceptive receptors provide feedback regarding position, such as that of the muscle
spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and Ruffini endings in joint capsules. Nociceptors
interpret pain, and thermoreceptors interpret temperature.1
Nerve Metabolism
Axoplasmic transport (ie, intracellular transport of substances along an axon) is possible by the
polarization of the neuron.
Proteins, which are created only in the cell body of a neuron, travel via antegrade transport
through the axon and dendrites of the neuron to support neural functions, such as action
potential propagation and neurotransmitter release.
Degradation products travel back to the cell body via retrograde transport. Several other
factors also travel to the cell body in retrograde fashion, including nerve-growth factors, some
viruses (eg, herpes simplex, rabies, polio), tetanus toxin, and horseradish peroxidase (used in
the laboratory to identify the location of a cell body in a dorsal root ganglion or in the spinal
cord).
The rate of axonal transport decreases with decreasing temperature and anoxia.

Nerve Metabolism
The neuron is the smallest functional unit of nerves and is composed of a cell body with
cytoplasmic extensions, including multiple dendritic processes to receive information
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:29 AM
AAOS | Biology and Function of Nerve
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002111
11/36

(afferent) and a single axonal process to transmit information (efferent). Inside of the cell
body, otherwise known as the soma, are the nucleus, neurofilaments, mitochondria,
lysosomes, and Nissl bodies surrounded by cytoplasm. The cell bodies of peripheral
nerves occasionally are located within the CNS. The axon originates from the soma at a
site called the axon hillock and travels distally as a peripheral extension. Each axon has a
thin outer layer called the axolemma, which is the cell membrane that encloses the
axoplasm and extends from the cell body along the entire length of the axon. The
axoplasm acts as a conduit for transport of substances to and from the cell body and
distal nerve terminals. Within the axon are many structures supporting its function,
including mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, lysosomes, vesicles, microtubules, and
neurofilaments. Schwann cells wrap around the axons and lay down myelin along the
axolemma.1
Embryology of the Nervous System
The nervous system (and skin) is formed by the ectoderm, which, with the mesoderm and
endoderm, is one of the three germ layers of embryonic tissue.
The ectoderm divides to form the neural tube, which gives rise to the brain, spinal cord, and
motor neurons; the neural crest, which evolves into afferent neurons; and the epidermal layer
of the skin.
The peripheral nervous system is divided into the autonomic nervous system; a purely motor
visceral system; and a mixed sensory and motor somatic system, which helps control voluntary
motion.
Axonal Growth and Development
Axonal growth and development are initially guided by different nerve growth factors.
N-cadherin and neural cell adhesion molecule are adhesive membrane glycoproteins that
are expressed on neural ectoderm and help guide growing axons.
Laminin and fibronectin are glycoproteins of the extracellular matrix that promote the
directional growth of nerve fibers.
Other factors thought to enhance nerve regeneration include nerve-growth factor, fibroblast
growth factor, ciliary neuronotrophic factor, and insulin-like growth factor.

Spinal Nerves
Spinal nerves are collections of axons that exit the spinal cord at distinct levels (8 cervical, 12
thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).
The efferent ventral root of a spinal nerve transmits information from the brain to muscle; the
afferent dorsal root carries signals from the periphery back to the CNS.
The cell bodies of afferent sensory nerves are in the dorsal root ganglion, which lies near the
point at which the spinal nerve exits the spinal cord (Figure 4).
The cell bodies of efferent motor nerves are in the anterior horn of the spinal cord.
Spinal nerves frequently collect into plexuses (cervical, brachial, lumbar) before branching.

Nerve Conduction and Biomechanics
Propagation of a Nerve Signal
The axon membrane of a neuron consists of a selectively permeable lipid bilayer that contains
gated ion channels and transmembrane pumps. These pumps derive their energy from
sodium/potassium adenosine triphosphate. The control of gated ion channels (sodium and
potassium) primarily is governed by electrical, chemical, and mechanical stimuli. The
sodium/potassium adenosine triphosphate–dependent pumps create an accumulation of
sodium ions outside the membrane, which is responsible for the negative resting potential
that exists within the axon membrane. If a stimulus causes the gated ion channels to open,
sodium flows rapidly into the axon, causing its depolarization.
Conduction of signals along an axon begins with action potentials, which are generated if the
axon membrane is depolarized beyond a critical threshold.
The rate at which an action potential is conducted along an axon depends on the size of the
axon and the presence of myelin; larger axons and myelinated axons carry action potentials
more rapidly than smaller or unmyelinated axons.
Within the nodes of Ranvier along the axon, dense collections of sodium channels propagate
the action potential, allowing saltatory (pulse-like) conduction between one node and the next.
Most peripheral motor and sensory nerves are myelinated; the axons of efferent motor nerves
are the most heavily myelinated. Autonomic nerve fibers and slow-pain fibers are examples of
unmyelinated nerves.

Propagation of a Nerve Signal
Nerves transmit signals through action potentials, by creating a transient reversal of
electrical potential across cell membranes. Membrane potential describes the
transmembrane distribution of charge, or, in other words, the relative charge inside of
the cell compared with the charge outside of the cell.6 The resting membrane potential
of a neuronal cell is −70 mV, with a relatively high concentration of sodium and chloride
ions in the extracellular fluid and a relatively high concentration of potassium ions in the
intracellular fluid. To initiate an action potential, a stimulus causes sodium ion channels
in the plasma membrane to open, resulting in passive inflow of positively charged
sodium ions into the cell and an increased (ie, less negative) membrane potential. Stimuli

9/3/26, 7:29 AM
AAOS | Biology and Function of Nerve
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002111
14/36

initiating this process can come from multiple sources, including neurotransmitters that
bind to and open ligand-gated sodium ion channels or physical stimulus, such as
pressure that is detected by sensory receptors and opens mechanical-gated sodium ion
channels.6,7 If the threshold potential of −55 mV is reached, voltage-gated sodium ion
channels open, allowing additional sodium ions to passively enter the cell driven by the
concentration gradient. The resulting membrane depolarization results in an action
potential; the positive current created passively travels down the axon, resulting in a
series of membrane depolarizations along the axon by the same process.6,8
Soon after membrane depolarization, sodium ion channels inactivate after a
predetermined period of time (approximately 1 ms) because of a conformational change
that blocks further passage of sodium ions through the open voltage-gated channels.6
Because of depolarization, voltage-gated potassium ion channels also open; these
channels require a higher threshold to activate than voltage-gated sodium ion channels
and, therefore, are slower to open.6 After potassium ion channels open, positively
charged potassium ions passively move out of the cell driven by concentration gradient,
resulting in membrane repolarization and, eventually, hyperpolarization. Repolarization
causes the voltage-gated sodium ion and potassium ion channels to deactivate and
close; hyperpolarization occurs because potassium ion channels are relatively slow to
deactivate.6 Additional action potentials are difficult to initiate until after potassium ion
channels close (relative refractory phase) and cannot occur until after sodium ion
channels recover from transient inactivation (absolute refractory phase).8 These
refractory phases ensure that action potentials are not able to propagate in a retrograde
fashion.6 An active sodium-potassium pump is required to restore the ionic composition
of the resting cell membrane, using adenosine triphosphate energy to move sodium ions
out of the cell and potassium ions into the cell, both against their concentration
gradients.9
 The rate that action potentials propagate down an axon, or conduction velocity, is
affected by the presence or absence of myelin sheath and the nerve fiber diameter, with
faster conduction occurring in myelinated nerve fibers with greater diameters.10 The
myelin sheath acts as insulation, preventing loss of current and increasing the speed of

15/36

travel. Conduction in myelinated fibers occurs via saltatory travel, during which action
potentials skip rapidly from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier.8,10 Larger nerve fibers
have longer internodes, resulting in increased distances of conduction between each
node of Ranvier during saltatory travel, which further increases conduction velocity.10
Myelinated fibers conduct at approximately 4.6 to 6 m/s per millimeter in diameter, with
larger diameter axons conducting at greater velocities compared with unmyelinated
fibers at approximately 1.7 m/s per millimeter in diameter.8
Multiple sclerosis and Guillain-Barré syndrome are examples of nervous system
diseases that cause demyelination and slowed nerve-conduction velocities.
Multiple sclerosis is a chronic (and occasionally remitting) neurologic disorder
characterized by the perivascular infiltration of inflammatory cells, followed by
damage to the myelin sheaths of nerves and to nerve fibers themselves. Problems
with motor control (eg, vision, strength, balance) and cognition develop in patients
with multiple sclerosis.
Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute, inflammatory condition affecting nerves and
spinal nerve roots (ie, a polyradiculoneuropathy). It is presumed to be an
autoimmune condition, typically triggered by a viral or bacterial infection that causes
the production of antibodies that attack the myelin sheath. The loss of myelin leads
to an acute impairment of sensory and motor nerve function, ranging in severity
from paresthesias and weakness to complete loss of sensation and paralysis.
The neuromuscular junction is a highly specialized region between the distal nerve
terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber. It consists of the presynaptic terminal or distal-
most end of a nerve fiber; a synaptic cleft, into which the nerve terminal releases
neurotransmitter substance; and a postsynaptic membrane, a part of the cell
membrane of a neuron or muscle fiber on which the neurotransmitter released by the
nerve terminal acts to produce a response (Figure 1, B).
The arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic terminal triggers the release of
acetylcholine from vesicles in the terminal.
Acetylcholine travels across the synaptic cleft and, after bound to receptors on the
postsynaptic membrane, causes depolarization of the motor end plate and
stimulation of the muscle fiber.
Biomechanics
Nerves are viscoelastic structures that respond to stress in a nonlinear manner.

If a nerve is stretched, it becomes ischemic before disrupting; for example, a nerve
may undergo ischemia at 15% strain and rupture at 20% strain.
The ultimate strain that can be endured by a nerve ranges from 20% to 60%.
Nerves can lengthen because of viscoelastic properties. Nerves also are able to glide
during excursion toward the site of elongation to relieve some of the tension. With
normal range of motion, the brachial plexus has a total excursion of approximately
50 mm with shoulder motion. The median and ulnar nerves have approximately 7.3
and 9.8 mm of excursion, respectively, at the elbow and 14.5 and 13.8 mm of
excursion, respectively, at the wrist. Mobility is more restricted at sites of nerve
branching and vessel penetration.1
Nerve Injury, Repair, and Healing
Response to Injury
Peripheral nerves respond to injury via an initial inflammatory response.
This response typically results in increased epineurial permeability and edema because the
vessels within the epineurium lack a blood-nerve barrier.
An injury that involves disruption (eg, crush, transection) that exposes the endoneurium
disrupts the blood-nerve barrier, increasing the permeability of the endoneurial capillaries.
Injury from ischemia and compression can increase endoneurial pressure, fluid edema, and
capillary permeability without affecting the perineurial vascular system.
In these cases, the positive fluid pressure inside the endoneurium affects blood flow,
decreasing nutrition and oxygen delivery to nerve cells and the removal of waste products
from them.
Persistent intraneural edema can diminish nerve function, as observed in patients with
chronic compressive neuropathy.

Neurapraxia
Neurapraxia is an immediate, localized blocking of neural conduction, with normal conduction
above and below the injury site.
Neurapraxias typically are reversible. Axon continuity is maintained, but local demyelination
and ischemia occur.
Mechanisms of injury causing neurapraxia include compression, traction, and contusion.
Axonotmesis
Axonotmesis involves axon disruption without the destruction of Schwann cells, the
perineurium, or the epineurium. The axon distal to the point of injury degenerates (Wallerian
degeneration).
Some nerve function may be recovered because nerve-fiber regeneration is guided by an
intact neural connective tissue layer (eg, intact endoneurium).
Mechanisms of injury causing axonotmesis include crush and forceful stretch.

Neurotmesis
Neurotmesis is complete disruption of a nerve.
No spontaneous recovery of the affected nerve can be expected.
Mechanisms of injury include open crush, violent stretch, and laceration.
Sunderland revised the Seddon classification of nerve injuries into the categories of
neurapraxia, axonotmesis, and neurotmesis by defining three subtypes of axonotmesis.1,4
Pathoanatomy of Injury
Laceration
If the continuity of a nerve is disrupted, the two nerve ends retract, the cell body of the neuron
swells, the nucleus is displaced peripherally, and chromatolysis (dispersion of basophilic Nissl
granules with relative eosinophilia of the cell body) occurs (Figure 5, A and B)
The nerve cell stops producing neurotransmitters and begins synthesizing proteins required
for axonal regeneration.
Wallerian degeneration distal to the site of injury begins within hours and is characterized by
axonal disorganization caused by proteolysis, followed by the breakdown of myelin.
Schwann cells become active in clearing myelin and axonal debris from the site of injury.

Compression
If a nerve is compressed, nerve fibers are deformed, local ischemia occurs, and vascular
permeability is increased.
Edema then affects the endoneurial environment, resulting in poor axonal transport and nerve
dysfunction.
If compression continues, the edema and dysfunction persist, and fibroblasts invade the
nerve, producing scar tissue, which impairs the gliding of nerve fascicles over one another in
joint flexion.
Tissue pressures as high as 30 mm Hg can cause paresthesias and increase the latency of
nerve conduction. A tissue pressure of 60 mm Hg can completely block nerve conduction.
Ischemia
After 15 minutes of anoxia, axonal transport stops.
Axonal transport can recover if reperfusion occurs within 12 to 24 hours.
Nerve Regeneration After Injury
With or without suture reapproximation of disrupted nerve ends, nerve regeneration begins
with axonal elongation across the zone of injury (Figure 5, C and D).
The zone of injury undergoes an ingrowth of capillaries and Schwann cells.
The Schwann cells migrate from the proximal and distal stumps of a disrupted axon or nerve
fiber into the gap created by the disruption and attempt to form columns (Büngner bands) to
guide the tip or growth cone of the axon or fiber.
The growth cone is sensitive to neurotrophic growth factors, such as nerve growth factor,
and to factors that promote the formation of neurites (axons or dendrites), such as laminin.
Distal reinnervation of muscle occurs only if the muscle has viable motor end plates that a
regenerating nerve can stimulate.
In the acute period after a nerve injury, muscle innervated by the injured nerve increases the
number of its motor end plates, seeking stimulation by the nerve.

Nerve Regeneration After Injury
Immediately after axonal injury, the axon distal to the site of trauma degenerates via a
process called Wallerian degeneration, described in 1850 by Augustus Waller.
Degeneration also occurs within the proximal stump for a variable distance. Schwann
cells and macrophages are recruited to the area and phagocytize the myelin and axonal
debris over 3 to 6 weeks, reducing tension within endoneurial tubes and the cross-
sectional areas of fascicles. Such changes can be evaluated histologically via various
techniques, such as the benchmark resin-embedded semithin section treated with the
use of toluidine blue staining11 (Figure 6). The basement membranes of Schwann cells
associated with the endoneurial tubes are left behind, and proliferating Schwann cells
align along these basement membranes. The persistence of the basal lamina serves as a
conduit during regeneration of nerve fibers, guiding axons toward the appropriate end
organs. During this process, the epineurial tissue does not undergo considerable
change.

The cell body undergoes a process called chromatolysis as early as several hours after
nerve injury, during which swelling of the cell body and nucleolus, morphologic changes
of the nucleus, and changes in cellular metabolism occur.12 The primary goal of
metabolism transitions from supporting nerve signal transmission to supporting nerve
regeneration, with an increase in synthesis of RNA, growth-associated proteins (eg,
growth-associated protein-43, tubulin, actin), lipids, and enzymes that peaks 2 to 3
weeks postinjury.11 Axons at the site of injury sprout into multiple regenerating axons;
timing of sprouting depends on the severity of injury. Neurotropism is the phenomenon
in which neurotropic factors present at the distal nerve stump of an injured nerve attract
regenerating axons to their appropriate targets. Although this process may guide
regeneration in physically separated nerve ends, it is less effective after nerve repair;
after nerve ends are reapproximated, regenerating axons typically take the path of least
resistance.

After injury of motor nerve fibers, the perimysium and epimysium thicken, and spindle
cells atrophy over 2 to 6 weeks. As fibrosis forms around motor nerve fibers, they
eventually fragment and lose synaptic contact with muscle fibers.12 Motor end plate
atrophy typically occurs within 12 to 24 months postinjury, at which point motor
reinnervation is no longer possible.
Management of Peripheral Nerve Injuries
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is appropriate for all neurapraxias and most axonotmeses.
During the recovery of a motor nerve serving a limb muscle, great care should be taken to
maintain the functionality and viability of the limb. Specifically, distal joints should be
mobilized, and distal muscle groups should be stretched or protectively splinted to avoid
contractures.
Neglect of the affected limb may result in osteopenia, joint stiffness, and muscle atrophy.
Nerve recovery can be monitored clinically via an advancing Tinel sign along the path of the
nerve. Serial nerve conduction and EMG studies also can be performed to monitor nerve
recovery.
Recovery of an injured sensory nerve occurs in the following sequence:
Pressure sense
Protective pain
Moving touch
Moving two-point discrimination
Static two-point discrimination
Threshold sensation (measured with the use of Semmes-Weinstein monofilament and
exposure to vibration)
Surgical Management
Prerequisites for nerve repair (neurorrhaphy) include a clean wound, a well-vascularized repair
bed, skeletal stability, and viable soft-tissue coverage.
Before repair, the disrupted nerve ends are sharply débrided of injured or devitalized nerve,
scar tissue, and fibrotic tissue to expose healthy nerve fascicles.

Repair performed within the first few days of injury is associated with distinct advantages
because disrupted nerves retract, scar tissue forms over time, and neuromas develop soon
after injury.
Immobilization of the joint above and below a nerve repair for 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively
prevents stress at the repair site.
The most effective repair technique for an injured nerve is an epineurial repair (ie, suture
repair of the epineurium only) performed via microsurgical instrumentation and technique.
In reapproximating the ends of an injured nerve during epineurial repair, care should be
taken to orient the nerve ends to match the fascicles as accurately as possible. This
technique typically minimizes scar formation.
Repair can be performed with the use of fine microsuture (such as 8-0 or 9-0) or with the use
of fibrin glue.
Repair should be performed with minimal tension on the nerve.
Group fascicular repair involves reapproximating fascicular groups via perineurial repair. This
technique is anatomically more precise than epineurial repair; however, it requires intraneural
dissection, which results in greater scar tissue formation and intraneural fibrosis, blocking
axonal regeneration.
Results of peripheral nerve repair vary.
Young patients who undergo early repair of distal single-function nerves performed with the
use of short nerve grafts or as direct repair have better outcomes than older patients who
undergo late repair of proximal, mixed nerves performed with the use of long nerve grafts.
The rate of nerve regeneration after repair also varies; historically, it has been estimated to
be 1 mm per day, which is approximately equal to the rate of axonal transport of
neurofilament proteins essential to nerve growth.
Muscular neurotization involves implanting the end of an injured nerve directly into the belly
of the muscle served by the nerve. This type of procedure may be particularly helpful for
reinnervating neighboring muscles after traumatic limb amputation.
Ideally, peripheral nerve repair is performed as soon as possible. Early repair is recommended
to avoid retraction of the nerve, making tensionless repair more difficult and avoiding end-
organ changes, such as muscle atrophy and fibrosis. Prerequisites are a clean wound, good
vascular supply, no crush component of the injury, and adequate soft-tissue coverage.13 Hentz
et al demonstrated in a primate model that nerve repair performed with modest tension
perform better than nerves fixed with the use of interfascicular grafts.14 Group fascicular
repair has not been shown to be superior to simple epineurial repair.15

Nerve grafting is performed if segmental defects in a nerve cannot be overcome via joint
flexion or nerve transposition. Nerve repair only made possible with a flexed joint will not
tolerate joint extension well after healing, potentially resulting in permanent joint stiffness.
Autografts are implanted in the same manner as that used in the primary repair of a nerve;
however, these grafts should be reversed to decrease axonal dispersion through the graft.
Nerve grafts may be cabled to increase their diameter to match the size of the injured nerve;
they also should be reversed to minimize the early arborization of regenerating nerve fibers.
The sural nerve is a common source of autograft and can be cut into parallel sections to
create a cable graft of greater diameter.
The use of nerve allografts is increasing.
Fresh allografts require immunosuppression and are infrequently used.
Cleansed or processed allografts do not require immunosuppression and do not involve a
donor site. In animal studies, these grafts have been shown to promote nerve-fiber
regeneration more densely across gaps than nerve conduits. Early clinical studies also have
demonstrated nerve healing across these allografts.16
In lieu of bridging a nerve gap with the use of an autograft or allograft, surgeons may use
biologic (vein graft) or bioabsorbable nerve conduits (collagen, polylactic acid, or porcine
submucosa extracellular matrix). Scaffolds and nerve growth factor carriers currently are
being implemented into these conduits to augment their efficacy.
Nerve graft is necessary for segmental defects. The three main options of nerve autograft are
cable, trunk, and vascular grafts. Cable grafts are multiple small-caliber nerves that are
oriented in parallel to fill a defect of a large nerve. Trunk grafts are mixed motor/sensory
nerves; however, these types of grafts typically are not associated with good results.
Vascularized nerve grafts usually are used only for brachial plexus injuries, given donor site
morbidity. Common donor grafts include sural nerve, posterior interosseous nerve, and
medial antebrachial nerve. Nerve allograft also is available; however, results are not equivalent
to those of autologous graft.13
Nerve conduits have been used for sensory nerve defects. Autogenous conduits consist of vein
graft that has been shown to result in success with grafts smaller than 3 cm. Bioabsorbable
conduits consist of collagen, polyglycolic acid, and caprolactone. Additional research on the
efficacy of these conduits is ongoing.16
Nerve transfers are an effective method for managing severe nerve injuries not amenable to
nerve grafting, such as cervical nerve root avulsions or large segmental nerve injuries.

To transfer a nerve from a site of its healthy functioning to a nonfunctioning nerve, intra-
fascicular dissection must be performed. In this procedure, a single fascicle without critical
end-organ/muscle function is isolated with the use of a nerve stimulator. The healthy donor
fascicle is released and is sutured to the cut end of the nonfunctioning recipient nerve.
An example of a nerve transfer is the transfer of a fascicle of a functioning ulnar nerve that
innervates the flexor carpi ulnaris to the musculocutaneous nerve branch to the biceps
muscle in a patient with brachial plexus palsy to restore active elbow flexion.
Nerve transfer can be reliably performed end to end; however, circumstances in which an
end-to-side nerve transfer may be performed also exist. End-to-side nerve healing occurs via
either terminal or collateral sprouting.
Nerve transfers are similar to tendon transfers in which nerves with nonessential function
are transferred to a denervated nerve to regain lost function. Nerve transfers commonly are
used for brachial plexus injuries in which traditional nerve repair is not feasible. The area of
injury may be quite proximal if repair occurs more than 12 to 18 months postinjury. By that
time, irreversible end-organ changes may have occurred. The advantage of the nerve
transfer is that it shortens the length that the nerve must regenerate by bringing the donor
nerve closer to the target organ.17 Contraindications to nerve transfer include superior
reconstruction options, excessive time from injury (usually more than 12 to 18 months),
and/or donor-nerve motor strength less than Medical Research Council grade M4.17
Diagnostic Studies
Overview
The primary tests used to evaluate the integrity of the peripheral nervous system are EMG and
nerve conduction velocity studies.
These tests assess the function of sensory nerves, motor nerves, and muscles to confirm
diagnoses of neuropathies and myopathies.
They also can differentiate causes of weakness, identify the level and severity of nerve injuries
or abnormalities of conduction, and demonstrate the existence of denervated muscle and its
reinnervation.

Quantification of the speed of conduction of an action potential requires knowledge of the
distance (in millimeters) across which the action potential travels and the time (in milliseconds)

transmission through nerves.

temperature increase sensory nerve action potential amplitude; increasing age decreases
sensory nerve action potential amplitude.

Motor Nerve Function
A motor nerve action potential is recorded in a muscle, in which multiple muscle fibers are
innervated by a single nerve. The information recorded is therefore called a compound muscle
action potential (CMAP).
The CMAP measures not only the speed over the course of a nerve of an impulse produced by
stimulation but also the transmission of the impulse through the neuromuscular junction and
its conduction through muscle fibers.
An F wave is the recorded signal of a late response from distal muscles during CMAP testing.
If a stimulus is applied to a nerve innervating a muscle, the signal travels in the typical
proximal-to-distal fashion along the nerve, toward the muscle; however, the nerve also may
conduct a separate and immediately sequential signal in a distal-to-proximal direction,
toward the cells of the anterior horn of the spinal cord.
With adequate stimulation, cells of the anterior horn may discharge another proximal-to-
distal impulse (such as an F wave), which is recorded after the initial CMAP.
Electromyography
EMG studies cover an entire motor unit (eg, anterior horn cell of the spinal cord, motor
neuron, and muscle) and involve measuring insertional activity, which is the activity of a
muscle if the needle electrode of an electromyograph is inserted into it; spontaneous activity
of the muscle; motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) of the muscle, which are characterized by
their duration, amplitude, and shape; and recruitment, which is the successive activation of
additional motor units on stimulation of a single motor unit. These studies do not measure or
assess sensory information.
Insertional activity is measured as the needle electrode is passed into the muscle belly.
Decreased insertional activity results from poor muscle viability, muscle fibrosis, or muscle
atrophy.
Increased insertional activity may be a sign of denervation or a primary muscle disorder (eg,
polymyositis, myopathy).
Spontaneous activity involves electrical discharges in muscle that occur without muscle
contraction and without movement of the testing needle.
Fibrillations are an example of abnormal spontaneous activity; they occur in denervated
muscle fibers and in some myopathies. The density of fibrillations is graded from 1+ to 4+;
however, their amplitude aids in understanding the time of occurrence of denervation of a

Fasciculations are spontaneous discharges of a single motor unit. They can be detected
clinically by placing an electrode on the skin. They occur in various neuromuscular disorders,
including the syndrome of benign fasciculations, chronic radiculopathies, peripheral
polyneuropathies, thyrotoxicosis, and overdose of anticholinesterase medications.
MUAPs can measure voluntary muscle activity.
The amplitude of an MUAP characterizes the density of the muscle fibers within the motor
unit in which the MUAP is measured.
The duration and shape of the wave produced by the MUAP are affected by the quality of
conduction. For example, the MUAP of a partly denervated motor unit will be prolonged in
duration and polyphasic in shape as the motor unit is reinnervated with axonal sprouting
(Figure 9). If no reinnervation occurs, no MUAP will be generated.
Recruitment also is measured via the rate of MUAP generation and can be used to understand
whether muscle weakness is the result of a decrease in the number of peripheral motor
neurons and motor units or the result of a central problem in recruitment because of a CNS
lesion, pain, or poor voluntary effort.

from muscles innervated by that nerve will be observed. Nerve excitability will diminish 1
to 3 days postinjury, along with reduction in the CMAP and compound nerve action

and further CNAP amplitude reduction exists in the sensory NCS. At 6 to 10 days

postinjury, and fibrillation potentials are observed 14 days postinjury. The full extent of a
nerve injury can only be assessed after the third week postinjury. In nerves with a severe
injury but that are not transected, proportional reduction in CMAP and CNAP amplitudes
occurs, and needle EMG reveals voluntary MUP in muscles innervated by injured nerves.
Initial nerve studies may reveal no MUPs on needle EMG because of conduction block;
however, a repeat study after 6 to 8 weeks may demonstrate a few small-amplitude,
polyphasic MUPs indicative of reinnervation.18
MRI
MRI may be a useful adjunct to electrodiagnostic studies in assessing various disorders of the
peripheral nervous system.
MRI can reveal changes in muscle from denervation. For example, chronic denervation will
show evidence of fatty atrophy.
High-resolution images with adequate contrast are required to emphasize peripheral nerve
anatomy and nerve morphology.
The studies that provide these images take advantage of differences in the MRI signal of
distinct intraneural tissues, resulting from differences in the water content and physical
structure of fascicles, perineurium, and epineurium.

Peripheral Nerve Pharmacology
Local Anesthetic Agents
These agents create a sensorimotor nerve block, causing transient numbness and paralysis by
temporarily disrupting the transmission of action potentials along axons.
Lidocaine, mepivacaine, and bupivacaine (amide-type agents) have different durations of
action based on their specific biochemistries, with lidocaine having the shortest duration of
action and bupivacaine the longest duration of action.
Type C nerve fibers (eg, cutaneous pain fibers) are the most susceptible to the effects of local
anesthetic agents, and A fibers (eg, motor axons and deep pressure sense) are the least
susceptible to the effects of local anesthetic agent.
Local anesthetic agents of the amide type are processed by the liver via cytochrome P450
enzyme into metabolites that are more water soluble than their parent compounds; these
metabolites are then excreted in the urine.
Epinephrine may be combined with these anesthetic agents for vasoconstriction.
This combination reduces the systemic absorption of local anesthetic agents from the
injection site by decreasing blood flow in the area around the site.
Epinephrine reduces the systemic blood levels of local anesthetic agents by as much as 30%.
Because epinephrine-induced local vasoconstriction causes less of a local anesthetic to be
absorbed systemically, it increases the local neuronal uptake of the anesthetic in the region
in which it is injected.
Lidocaine with epinephrine was initially thought to be dangerous for use in the hand. A
recent study by Lalonde and Martin19 demonstrated its safety in multiple procedures in
the hand and fingers; in patients in whom vasoconstriction needs to be reversed,
phentolamine, an alpha antagonist, is used.
Botulinum Toxin
Botulinum toxin, produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, can be injected into
muscle to manage muscular spasticity.
The toxin works at the level of the neuromuscular junction. If injected into muscle, it blocks the
release of acetylcholine from axon terminals at the presynaptic clefts of the neuromuscular
junction, preventing acetylcholine from reaching the motor end plate and triggering muscle
contraction. Therefore, it causes chemical denervation and muscle paralysis.
